questions.original: What does privacy mean to you, and how private a person are you?
questions.paraphrased: What is something you keep private that people might be surprised about?

vocab.definition: the right to keep personal things to yourself
a limit on what you share with others

possibleAnswers: Privacy is my personal space — I am selective about what I share.
I am quite open, but some things stay for my closest people.
I respect privacy deeply, both mine and other people's.

questions.original: What is something you would never post on social media?
questions.paraphrased: What makes it off-limits for you?
possibleAnswers: My home address — some things should stay private.
Embarrassing moments — the internet never forgets.
Anything about my family's problems.

questions.original: Do you think people share too much about their lives online?
questions.paraphrased: What is the line between sharing and over-sharing?

vocab.definition: to share more than is wise or appropriate
the people who see what you post

possibleAnswers: Sometimes people forget who their audience is.
A little mystery is healthy.
Share what you would say in a crowded room.

questions.original: How do you decide what to keep private in a new friendship?
questions.paraphrased: What earns the right to know the deeper things about you?

vocab.definition: the belief that someone is reliable and honest

possibleAnswers: Trust builds gradually — I share in layers.
I watch how they treat other people's secrets.
Time and consistency earn deeper trust.

questions.original: Is privacy a modern worry, or have people always cared about it?
questions.paraphrased: What did privacy look like before the internet?

vocab.definition: a period of time with particular features

possibleAnswers: The internet made privacy a bigger conversation.
People always wanted private lives — technology changed the scale.
In small villages everyone knew everything — different, not better.

questions.original: What is one thing you would want companies to do better with your data?
questions.paraphrased: How would that change your trust in them?

vocab.definition: open and clear about what you do

possibleAnswers: Tell me simply what they collect and why.
Let me delete my data easily.
Transparency would earn my trust instantly.

questions.original: How careful are you with your passwords and personal information?
questions.paraphrased: What is your best habit for staying safe online?

vocab.definition: a secret word that lets you into an account

possibleAnswers: I use different passwords and change them regularly.
Two-factor authentication is my non-negotiable.
I never click links I did not expect.

questions.original: Do you think facial recognition and fingerprint logins are convenient or worrying?
questions.paraphrased: What is the trade-off between ease and privacy?
possibleAnswers: Convenient — but I wonder who has the data.
It is fine for my phone, less fine on every camera.
The ease is real; the privacy question is real too.

questions.original: What would you do if you found out your personal information had leaked online?
questions.paraphrased: What is your first move to protect yourself?

vocab.definition: information that gets out without permission

possibleAnswers: Change passwords immediately, starting with email.
Check what exactly was exposed, then act.
Contact the service and monitor my accounts.

questions.original: What is something about your life you are glad is not public?
questions.paraphrased: Why is it better kept private?
possibleAnswers: My morning routine — some things need no audience.
My quiet struggles — I share them with people, not platforms.
Privacy lets me be fully myself without performance.

questions.original: What is the role of the police in an ideal society?
questions.paraphrased: How is that role different from what you see in reality?

vocab.definition: the people living together in an area

possibleAnswers: To protect and serve the community fairly.
To keep peace, not just enforce rules.
Ideally they would be part of the community, not apart from it.

questions.original: Do you feel the police in your country are generally trusted?
questions.paraphrased: What builds trust — or breaks it — between police and the public?

vocab.definition: believed to be honest and reliable

possibleAnswers: Trust grows when they treat everyone fairly.
Transparency and honesty build public trust.
Trust is fragile — one unfair act can break it.

questions.original: How would you explain the work of the police to a child?
questions.paraphrased: What would you tell them about calling for help?

vocab.definition: a dangerous situation needing urgent help

possibleAnswers: They are people who help when there is a problem.
In an emergency, they are the ones to call.
They keep the streets safe so everyone can live peacefully.

questions.original: What qualities do you think a good police officer needs?
questions.paraphrased: Which of those do you think are hardest to train?

vocab.definition: the ability to make good decisions

possibleAnswers: Calm under pressure and good judgement.
Empathy — the ability to see the human in every situation.
Patience and the courage to de-escalate.

questions.original: Have you or someone you know ever needed police help? What happened?
questions.paraphrased: How did that experience shape your view of them?
possibleAnswers: A family member was helped quickly after an accident — we were grateful.
I saw them calm a difficult situation peacefully.
One experience can shape your whole view.

questions.original: Do you think police officers have a stressful job?
questions.paraphrased: What makes it stressful, and how could that be reduced?
possibleAnswers: Extremely — they see difficult situations daily.
They need mental health support like anyone else.
Better training and support would reduce the stress.

questions.original: What is the difference between a police force and a community?
questions.paraphrased: How can they work better together?
possibleAnswers: The best safety comes from police and community cooperating.
Police work best when they know the people they serve.
Trust is a two-way street.

questions.original: If you could change one thing about how policing works, what would it be?
questions.paraphrased: How would that change help ordinary people?
possibleAnswers: More focus on prevention and community ties.
Better training in calming difficult situations.
More transparency about how decisions are made.

questions.original: How do films and TV shape how we see the police?
questions.paraphrased: What is different in real life compared to the screen?

vocab.definition: to show someone in a particular way

possibleAnswers: TV shows the action, not the paperwork and patience.
Real policing is mostly calm problem-solving.
Dramas make it exciting; reality is more human.

questions.original: What does 'respect' for the police look like in daily life?
questions.paraphrased: What does the police do to earn that respect?

vocab.definition: to get something through your actions

possibleAnswers: Respect flows both ways — it is earned by fairness.
A polite interaction builds respect instantly.
Respect means cooperating and being treated fairly in return.

questions.original: Would you ever consider working as a police officer?
questions.paraphrased: What would attract you to it, and what would give you pause?

vocab.definition: a job you do for a long time

possibleAnswers: Helping people appeals to me, though it is challenging.
The responsibility is big — that would give me pause.
I would consider community roles within policing.

questions.original: What is a question about the police that people rarely ask?
questions.paraphrased: Why is it hard to ask, and why does it matter?
possibleAnswers: How do officers feel after a hard day?
What training do they wish they had more of?
How do they balance the law with human judgement?

questions.original: What is a law you think is fair, and why?
questions.paraphrased: What would happen if that law did not exist?

vocab.definition: a rule made by a government

possibleAnswers: Laws protecting children are obviously fair.
Traffic laws keep everyone safer — that is fair.
Fair laws protect the vulnerable.

questions.original: What is a law you would change if you could?
questions.paraphrased: How would life improve for people if it changed?
possibleAnswers: Some laws feel outdated and need a modern review.
I would make certain penalties focus on repair, not punishment.
Laws should reflect how people actually live now.

questions.original: What is the difference between a fair law and a fair outcome?
questions.paraphrased: Can the law be fair even when life is not?
possibleAnswers: A fair law tries to create fair outcomes.
Justice considers the person, not just the rule.
They aim for the same thing — fairness for everyone.

questions.original: Have you ever witnessed something legal that felt wrong?
questions.paraphrased: What is the difference between legal and ethical?
possibleAnswers: Legal and ethical are not always the same.
Something can be within the rules but still feel wrong.
Laws lag behind ethics sometimes.

questions.original: Why do you think people follow the law even when nobody is watching?
questions.paraphrased: What keeps most people honest?

vocab.definition: people living together in a community

possibleAnswers: Most people are honest by nature.
We follow laws because they keep society working.
Our own sense of right and wrong guides us.

questions.original: What is your opinion on giving people a second chance after breaking the law?
questions.paraphrased: What should the balance be between punishment and rehabilitation?

vocab.definition: a new opportunity after a mistake
helping someone return to normal life

possibleAnswers: Everyone deserves a path back — rehabilitation matters.
Second chances work when people take responsibility.
Society benefits when people can rebuild their lives.

questions.original: Do you think courts are fair to everyone in your country?
questions.paraphrased: What could make the justice system fairer?

vocab.definition: the place where laws are judged

possibleAnswers: The ideal is fair; reality is more complex.
Equal access to good lawyers would help.
Fairness grows with transparency.

questions.original: How do you think laws should change as technology changes?
questions.paraphrased: What new technology needs new rules the most?

vocab.definition: to change to fit new situations

possibleAnswers: Privacy rules need to catch up with technology.
AI needs clear laws about fairness and responsibility.
Laws must adapt or they become meaningless.

questions.original: What would you want a judge to consider before deciding a case?
questions.paraphrased: What makes a decision truly fair in your eyes?

vocab.definition: a person who decides cases in court

possibleAnswers: The circumstances behind the action, not just the action.
The impact on the people involved.
Fairness, consistency, and human understanding.

questions.original: What is one thing you would teach young people about the law?
questions.paraphrased: Why does understanding the law matter for everyone?

vocab.definition: what you are legally allowed to do or have

possibleAnswers: Know your basic rights — they protect you.
The law is there to protect you too, not just restrict.
Understanding the law helps you participate in society.

questions.original: Do you think punishments should focus on punishment or on helping people change?
questions.paraphrased: What outcome is best for everyone in the long run?

vocab.definition: a penalty for doing something wrong

possibleAnswers: Helping people change reduces future harm.
A balance: accountability plus a path forward.
Society is safer when people can turn their lives around.

questions.original: What does politics mean to you in your daily life?
questions.paraphrased: How does it affect you without you even noticing?

vocab.definition: the activities of government and public life

possibleAnswers: It shapes the roads, schools and services I use.
Decisions made far away affect my daily choices.
Politics is how a society decides what matters.

questions.original: What is one political decision that improved life in your country?
questions.paraphrased: How did you notice the improvement in your own life?
possibleAnswers: Better public transport changed how I move around.
A policy that protected jobs helped my whole town.
Cleaner energy rules improved the air I breathe.

questions.original: How do you stay informed about politics without feeling overwhelmed?
questions.paraphrased: What is your personal news habit?

vocab.definition: feeling there is too much to handle

possibleAnswers: I read one reliable source a day, then stop.
I focus on issues that affect my life directly.
I check the news in the morning, not all day.

questions.original: What qualities do you think a good political leader needs?
questions.paraphrased: Which quality is most important to you personally?

vocab.definition: a person who guides or directs others
the quality of telling the truth

possibleAnswers: Honesty and the courage to make hard decisions.
Listening to people, not just their own party.
Long-term thinking beyond the next election.

questions.original: Do you think it is important for young people to vote?
questions.paraphrased: What would you say to a young person who thinks their vote does not matter?

vocab.definition: to speak and act for others

possibleAnswers: Absolutely — decisions today shape their future.
Your voice matters, and votes add up.
If you do not vote, others decide for you.

questions.original: How do you discuss politics with people who disagree with you?
questions.paraphrased: What makes those conversations productive instead of painful?
possibleAnswers: I listen first and look for common values.
I keep it respectful — the person matters more than the argument.
I focus on issues, not personal attacks.

questions.original: What is a political issue you care about that affects your generation?
questions.paraphrased: Why does it matter so much to you?

vocab.definition: people born around the same time

possibleAnswers: The environment — my generation inherits the planet.
Affordable housing — it shapes whether we can build lives.
Education and jobs — they determine our future.

questions.original: Do you believe politicians can change the world for the better?
questions.paraphrased: What gives you hope, and what makes you sceptical?

vocab.definition: doubting that something is true or good

possibleAnswers: Some genuinely try — good policy changes lives.
I am hopeful but watch actions, not promises.
Change usually comes from people pushing leaders.

questions.original: What is the difference between a good politician and a good leader?
questions.paraphrased: Can one person be both?
possibleAnswers: A politician manages; a leader inspires.
The best ones are both — skilled and genuine.
Leadership is about people; politics is about process.

questions.original: How do you think politics will change in the next twenty years?
questions.paraphrased: What role will technology and young people play?
possibleAnswers: Young people will push for more transparency.
Technology will change how campaigns and decisions work.
The issues will shift, but the core stays: people's lives.

questions.original: What is one political conversation you think everyone should have?
questions.paraphrased: Why is it important, even if it is difficult?
possibleAnswers: How to disagree without becoming enemies.
How we balance individual freedom and common good.
What kind of future we want for the next generation.

questions.original: What would you do if you were in charge of your country for one day?
questions.paraphrased: What one decision would you make, and why?
possibleAnswers: Invest in education — it fixes most other problems.
Make mental health care accessible to everyone.
Listen to citizens before making any big change.

questions.original: How do you feel about the way politics is reported in the news?
questions.paraphrased: What would fairer coverage look like?
possibleAnswers: It is often loud and divided — nuance gets lost.
Fair coverage would explain issues, not just clashes.
I wish the news focused on solutions too.

questions.original: What is something politicians from different sides could agree on?
questions.paraphrased: What common ground exists?

vocab.definition: things people share and agree about

possibleAnswers: Everyone wants their children to be safe and healthy.
Most agree that education matters.
A strong economy helps everyone — that is common ground.

questions.original: What does being politically informed mean to you?
questions.paraphrased: Is it about facts, understanding, or action?

vocab.definition: to grasp the meaning of something

possibleAnswers: Knowing the facts and how they affect people.
Understanding the issues deeply, not just headlines.
Being informed enough to make good decisions.

questions.original: What is a political promise you wish leaders would make?
questions.paraphrased: What would that promise mean for ordinary people?

vocab.definition: a statement that you will do something

possibleAnswers: A promise to listen to all citizens, not just supporters.
A promise to be honest even when it is hard.
A promise to focus on long-term good over short-term gain.

questions.original: How do you keep hope in politics when things feel divided?
questions.paraphrased: What gives you optimism?

vocab.definition: a feeling that good things will happen
a positive view of the future

possibleAnswers: I focus on local change I can see and support.
History shows societies can improve over time.
Ordinary people doing good gives me hope.

questions.original: What is one political topic you would love to understand better?
questions.paraphrased: What is the first step you would take to learn about it?
possibleAnswers: How budgets really work — where money goes.
How international relations affect my country.
I would start with a good book or documentary.

questions.original: What do you think poverty means beyond not having money?
questions.paraphrased: What does it take away that money cannot always fix?

vocab.definition: the state of being very poor
a chance to do something good

possibleAnswers: It limits opportunities and choices.
It can take away hope and security.
It is about access — to education, health, and chances.

questions.original: What is something communities do to help people in difficult times?
questions.paraphrased: Have you seen kindness like this where you live?
possibleAnswers: Food banks and community kitchens help many families.
Neighbours look out for each other in hard times.
Small acts of support add up to real change.

questions.original: What do you think are the main causes of poverty in the world?
questions.paraphrased: Which cause do you think is most preventable?

vocab.definition: able to be stopped before it happens

possibleAnswers: Lack of access to education and opportunity.
Unfair systems that keep people from rising.
Crises — health, climate, conflict — hit the poorest hardest.

questions.original: How can education help break the cycle of poverty?
questions.paraphrased: What makes education so powerful?

vocab.definition: a chance to improve your life

possibleAnswers: Education opens doors that poverty keeps closed.
It gives people the tools to build a better future.
One educated generation can change a family's path.

questions.original: What is a small thing an individual can do to help someone struggling?
questions.paraphrased: What have you done, or seen someone do, that made a difference?
possibleAnswers: Give without judgement — a meal, a coffee, a ride.
Volunteer an hour at a local charity.
Listen and treat people with dignity.

questions.original: Do you think governments or charities are more effective at fighting poverty?
questions.paraphrased: What is each better at?

vocab.definition: a plan of action by a government

possibleAnswers: Governments can create lasting change through policy.
Charities are quick and personal.
They work best together.

questions.original: What is something about poverty that people who have never experienced it misunderstand?
questions.paraphrased: What would you want them to know?
possibleAnswers: It is not about laziness — it is often circumstance.
Hard work alone does not always escape poverty.
People in poverty have the same dreams as anyone.

questions.original: What is a skill or resource that can change someone's future?
questions.paraphrased: What would you share with someone starting from nothing?
possibleAnswers: A practical skill that pays — like languages or trades.
Access to information and mentorship.
Someone who believes in you.

questions.original: How does poverty affect children differently from adults?
questions.paraphrased: What do children need most when times are hard?

vocab.definition: the time when you are a child
the process of growing and learning

possibleAnswers: Children need stability and hope to grow well.
Poverty can limit a child's chances before they begin.
Schools and meals programs make a huge difference.

questions.original: What is a myth about poverty you would like to correct?
questions.paraphrased: What is the reality behind it?
possibleAnswers: That poor people are not working hard — many work multiple jobs.
That it only happens in other countries.
That it is permanent — people escape poverty every day.

questions.original: What would a fairer world look like when it comes to money?
questions.paraphrased: What is the first step towards it?
possibleAnswers: Everyone having their basic needs met.
Equal chances to learn and work.
A world where luck matters less than effort.

questions.original: What is something you appreciate more because you know it is not available to everyone?
questions.paraphrased: What simple things do you value because of that awareness?

vocab.definition: to recognise the value of something

possibleAnswers: Clean water and hot meals — small things, huge value.
A warm home and a safe bed.
Education — it is a privilege for many.

questions.original: What do you think war takes away from ordinary people that money cannot replace?
questions.paraphrased: What is the first thing you would protect if conflict ever came near your home?
possibleAnswers: War takes safety, homes and the feeling of a normal tomorrow.
It takes childhoods and peace of mind.
I would protect my family and our community first.

questions.original: Why do you think conflicts still happen in a world with so many resources?
questions.paraphrased: What do you think is usually underneath the stated reasons?

vocab.definition: something valuable like land, money or energy

possibleAnswers: Power and resources are often the real drivers.
Fear and mistrust between groups fuel conflicts.
History shows that understanding can prevent many wars.

questions.original: Do you think peace is something countries build actively, or just the absence of war?
questions.paraphrased: What does actively building peace look like?

vocab.definition: the skill of managing relations between countries

possibleAnswers: Peace is active — it needs diplomacy and trust-building.
It is more than no war; it is people living well together.
Trade, education and dialogue build peace daily.

questions.original: What do you think can be learned from the stories of people who lived through wars?
questions.paraphrased: What story about war has stayed with you?

vocab.definition: someone who lived through a disaster

possibleAnswers: That ordinary people show extraordinary strength.
That humanity and kindness survive even in the darkest times.
Their stories remind us why peace matters.

questions.original: How do films and news shape the way we understand war?
questions.paraphrased: What do you think they leave out?

vocab.definition: to show something in a particular way

possibleAnswers: Films show heroics; real war is mostly loss and waiting.
News shows numbers; the human stories get lost.
We need both — facts and faces.

questions.original: What does 'peace' mean in your daily life?
questions.paraphrased: What small things make you feel peaceful?
possibleAnswers: Walking home safely in the evening.
A quiet morning with coffee and no alarms.
Peace is ordinary life continuing without fear.

questions.original: Do you think understanding history helps prevent future conflicts?
questions.paraphrased: What lesson from history do you think is most important?
possibleAnswers: Yes — those who forget history repeat it.
Understanding the roots of conflict helps avoid them.
History teaches us what peace requires.

questions.original: How do you think technology changes the nature of conflicts?
questions.paraphrased: What is different about modern conflict compared to the past?

vocab.definition: related to computers and the internet

possibleAnswers: Cyber attacks can now hit without a single soldier.
Information itself has become a battlefield.
Technology changes the tools, not the human cost.

questions.original: What role do you think ordinary citizens play in keeping peace?
questions.paraphrased: What can neighbours, communities and friends do?

vocab.definition: a member of a community or country

possibleAnswers: Refusing to hate groups of people is a start.
Communities that know each other are harder to divide.
Everyday kindness between people builds peace.

questions.original: If you could send one message to world leaders about peace, what would it be?
questions.paraphrased: What would you want them to remember?
possibleAnswers: The people who suffer are never the ones who decide.
Talk longer before acting — every hour of peace matters.
Ordinary lives are the real treasure.

questions.original: What is a story of reconciliation you have heard that gives you hope?
questions.paraphrased: What made that healing possible?

vocab.definition: the process of becoming whole again

possibleAnswers: Former enemies meeting to rebuild their town together.
A country that chose truth-telling over revenge.
Healing becomes possible when people listen to each other.

questions.original: How do you think the next generation will look at the wars of today?
questions.paraphrased: What do you hope they learn from them?

vocab.definition: people born around the same time

possibleAnswers: I hope they see how avoidable most conflicts are.
They will ask why we could not find another way.
Their job is to build what we failed to protect.

questions.original: What is one thing you would never want to live through?
questions.paraphrased: What does that fear tell you about what you value?
possibleAnswers: Losing my home and everything familiar.
Watching the people I love be unsafe.
It tells me peace is the most precious thing I have.

questions.original: What role does faith or spirituality play in people's lives, whether they follow a religion or not?
questions.paraphrased: What do people look for in religion or belief?

vocab.definition: a sense of meaning beyond the physical world

possibleAnswers: It gives people community, comfort and meaning.
Even non-religious people seek purpose and connection.
Faith is a way of making sense of life.

questions.original: How do different faiths and beliefs coexist in your country?
questions.paraphrased: What makes that coexistence work — or difficult?
possibleAnswers: Respect and curiosity make coexistence work.
Shared festivals and food help people connect.
It works when people see each other as neighbours first.

questions.original: What is something about religion that people misunderstand?
questions.paraphrased: What would you want them to know?

vocab.definition: made up of many different kinds

possibleAnswers: Religions are diverse — one person is not all of them.
Faith is personal, not a label for judging.
Believers are as varied as anyone else.

questions.original: Do you think religion is more about community or about personal belief?
questions.paraphrased: What do you think draws people in — the people or the beliefs?

vocab.definition: a group of people who share something
something you hold to be true

possibleAnswers: For many, the community is what keeps them.
The beliefs give meaning; the community gives support.
Both — they feed each other.

questions.original: How do families pass on faith, and how do children decide for themselves?
questions.paraphrased: At what age should people choose their own beliefs?

vocab.definition: to give something to the next generation

possibleAnswers: Families share traditions, but children should find their own path.
Explaining without forcing lets beliefs grow naturally.
Respect the choice either way.

questions.original: What is a tradition or celebration from a faith that you find beautiful?
questions.paraphrased: What does it celebrate, and what does it mean to those who keep it?

vocab.definition: a special event to mark something

possibleAnswers: Light festivals — they symbolise hope winning over darkness.
Communal meals that welcome everyone.
Moments of quiet reflection that slow life down.

questions.original: Should religion be taught in schools, and how?
questions.paraphrased: What is the difference between teaching religion and teaching about religion?

vocab.definition: to grasp the meaning of something

possibleAnswers: Learning about religions builds understanding, not belief.
Children should learn what faith means to different people.
Knowledge of each other's beliefs reduces prejudice.

questions.original: How do you think faith and science can coexist?
questions.paraphrased: What does each offer that the other does not?

vocab.definition: the study of the natural world

possibleAnswers: Science explains how; faith explores why.
Many people hold both without conflict.
They answer different questions.

questions.original: What is a question about faith that you have always wondered about?
questions.paraphrased: Who could you ask, and how would you find an answer?
possibleAnswers: Why bad things happen to good people.
What gives life meaning beyond everyday routines.
I would ask someone of that faith directly — respectfully.

questions.original: How do people find meaning in life without religion?
questions.paraphrased: What gives life purpose for non-religious people?
possibleAnswers: Family, work, art and helping others all give meaning.
Nature and connection can feel deeply spiritual.
Meaning is personal — everyone builds their own.

questions.original: What is the difference between respecting a religion and following it?
questions.paraphrased: Why can you do one without the other?

vocab.definition: to value something even if you differ

possibleAnswers: Respect means honouring what matters to others.
You can respect a faith without sharing its beliefs.
Respect is the foundation of living together.

questions.original: What can people of different beliefs learn from each other?
questions.paraphrased: What is a value that most faiths share?
possibleAnswers: Most faiths teach kindness and looking after others.
Generosity and forgiveness appear across traditions.
The shared values are bigger than the differences.

questions.original: How do you celebrate or reflect at important moments in life?
questions.paraphrased: What rituals — religious or not — mark your big moments?
possibleAnswers: I gather the people I love — that is my ritual.
A quiet walk helps me reflect on big changes.
Traditions, old or new, anchor important moments.

questions.original: What would you tell a child who asks why some people believe different things?
questions.paraphrased: How would you explain belief and difference simply?
possibleAnswers: People find meaning in different ways — that is beautiful.
Like favourite foods, beliefs differ but deserve respect.
The important thing is how we treat each other.

questions.original: What is a saying from your culture that you live by?
questions.paraphrased: Where did you first hear it, and what does it mean to you?

vocab.definition: a short wise phrase people repeat

possibleAnswers: My grandmother always said: slow and steady wins the race.
In my country we say: shared bread is never wasted.
It reminds me what my family values.

questions.original: Do you think 'fortune favours the bold' is true?
questions.paraphrased: What is a bold decision that paid off for you or someone you know?

vocab.definition: brave and willing to take risks

possibleAnswers: It has been true for me — the risks I took opened doors.
Boldness works when it comes with preparation.
My friend moved abroad on a whim — best decision ever.

questions.original: What do you think 'actions speak louder than words' really means?
questions.paraphrased: When has someone shown you more than they told you?

vocab.definition: to show that something is true

possibleAnswers: People remember what you did, not what you promised.
A friend who shows up proves more than one who says 'call me'.
Behaviour is the truest message.

questions.original: Is it true that 'the best things in life are free'?
questions.paraphrased: What free things matter most to you?
possibleAnswers: Sunrises, laughter and friendship — all free.
The best moments rarely cost money.
A walk with someone you love is priceless.

questions.original: What is your opinion of 'if it is not broken, do not fix it'?
questions.paraphrased: When is it wise to leave things alone, and when should we improve them?

vocab.definition: the chance of something going wrong

possibleAnswers: Good advice for things that work — don't risk them.
But some things work and could still be better.
